notations: Timothy Williamson, Knowledge and Its Limits

sources.note: External philosophy-of-knowledge book cited in the DDD consolidation as the source of TRUE != BELIEVED != KNOWN, ASSERTED != ACCEPTED != TRUE, CONFIDENCE != TRUTH, UNKNOWN != FALSE, and the principle that knowledge has epistemic requirements plus intrinsic limits on what can be known; not separately extracted at length elsewhere in this batch.

rows.anchor: TRUE != BELIEVED != KNOWN / ASSERTED != ACCEPTED != TRUE / CONFIDENCE != TRUTH / UNKNOWN != FALSE ... Absence of knowledge must not be represented as falsehood.
rows.statement: Williamson's contribution: knowledge is not whatever an agent believes, has epistemic requirements and intrinsic limits; motivates an explicit state vocabulary (UNKNOWN, ABSENT, INSUFFICIENT, QUESTIONABLE, CONFLICTED, REJECTED, VALIDATED, SUPERSEDED, WITHDRAWN) with the exact governed vocabulary left as a domain-law question.
invariants: Absence of knowledge must not be represented as falsehood.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS must never silently turn "supported" or "probable" into "known."
rows.statement: Knowledge is factive: a factive attitude can only be directed toward truths; Williamson treats knowing as the most general factive stative attitude, distinct from believed(P)/supported(P)/probable(P)/asserted(P), all of which 'may be false' while known(P) is factive. This should be a Kernel-level safeguard: never silently convert 'supported' or 'probable' into 'known'.

rows.anchor: Williamson rejects the assumption that knowledge can be completely separated into an internal mental part and an external-world part... he explicitly describes knowledge as broad
rows.statement: Knowledge is broad: K_A(P) depends not only on A's internal representation but on the external world, context, object of knowledge, and relevant environment. This revises the earlier Agent->projection->Knowledge Space model: the agent does not invent the space, the agent's knowledge is constitutively connected to the space (KNOWLEDGE SPACE Ω -> external world/social reality/semantic structures -> participant/agent -> capacity+access -> epistemic state).

lineage_claims.quote: was actually backwards in one sense

rows.anchor: Capacity is not knowledge.
rows.statement: A Williamson-inspired correction to the earlier 'knowledge might be a capacity to write information and define its scope' idea: capacity is not knowledge. A system can have high representation capacity (an LLM generating text, a database storing petabytes) without knowing anything. Instead: capacity determines what a participant can potentially represent/investigate/distinguish/communicate; knowledge is a factive epistemic relation/state involving the participant and the external target (CAPACITY -> access/observation/reasoning -> epistemic state -> KNOWLEDGE).

lineage_claims.target: earlier proposal 'knowledge might be a capacity to write information and define its scope'
lineage_claims.quote: I would now make a Williamson-inspired correction.

rows.anchor: He argues for the **primeness** of knowledge and warns against decomposing it into composite conditions when doing so loses explanatory generality.
rows.statement: Knowledge may be prime (non-composite): a maximally detailed decomposition can make an explanation worse by destroying useful generalization. This strengthens the earlier Merricks 'non-redundant work' principle (a candidate primitive deserves first-class status if removing it destroys non-redundant capability) into two tests: the Reduction test ('Can X be reconstructed?') and the Primeness test ('Does treating X as a composite destroy explanatory/general structure?').

lineage_claims.quote: Williamson strengthens it

rows.anchor: Williamson argues that people are not always in a position to know whether they know something. He calls the mistaken assumption that important mental conditions are cognitively transparent **luminosity** and argues against it.
rows.statement: Knowledge is not luminous (anti-luminosity): KnowledgeOS cannot assume a participant can perfectly report the state of its own knowledge. 'Agent says I know P' is itself an assertion requiring evaluation; 'Agent says I don't know P' does not necessarily prove P is outside its epistemic capacity. This is a major correction to the previous model of UNKNOWN, requiring KnowledgeOS to distinguish KNOWLEDGE / KNOWLEDGE ABOUT KNOWLEDGE (K_A(K_A(P))) / SELF-ASSESSMENT / EXTERNAL ASSESSMENT / COMPUTATIONAL ESTIMATE as non-equivalent layers, with the second not automatically following from the first.

lineage_claims.quote: This is a major correction to our previous model of `UNKNOWN`.

rows.anchor: The agent's **self-report of knowledge** is therefore an object of analysis, not a privileged oracle.
rows.statement: For an AI agent claiming 'I know that the architecture decision is valid', KnowledgeOS should be able to represent P, the AI's claim knows(P), the supporting evidence, an external assessment (e.g. 'insufficient'), and the actual status ('unresolved') separately — the agent's self-report of knowledge is an object of analysis, not a privileged oracle.

rows.anchor: Williamson's Chapter 5 investigates margins and "close possibilities."
rows.statement: Knowledge has a margin: an agent may know P under ordinary circumstances but not under arbitrary tiny variations, so knowledge is not simply a point (TRUE) but can have a 'neighbourhood of epistemic safety'. Proposed quantity M(P,A,C) represents the size/structure of the range of relevant variations under which the knowledge attribution remains stable (not a final formula) — high margin means knowledge remains stable under nearby changes, low margin means small changes may destroy knowledge. This connects the topological lens to epistemology: 'What kinds of changes would invalidate the knowledge attribution?'

rows.anchor: Williamson discusses contextual variation in epistemic standards but does not reduce truth/knowledge to arbitrary subjective standards.
rows.statement: Knowledge is contextual but not arbitrarily relative: different epistemic contexts (S_t^A, S_t^B, S_t^G) can differ in their knowledge attributions, but this does not mean 'everything is equally true' — different knowledge attributions still point to the same underlying Knowledge Space, supporting the idea that different participants are oriented toward the same infinite space.

rows.anchor: Williamson separates causal basis from evidential basis.
rows.statement: Cause of belief is not the same as evidence for belief: a perceptual process can be probabilistically caused by the environment without the resulting evidence itself being probabilistic in the same way. This is a non-collapse rule — KnowledgeOS must preserve both relationships (causal basis, evidential basis) separately.

rows.anchor: Williamson's Chapters 9–10 develop the idea that **knowledge itself can function as evidence**, and he explicitly identifies one's evidence with what one knows within his framework.
rows.statement: Knowledge can be evidence (E=K): observation -> knowledge -> evidence for another proposition -> new knowledge, a recursive structure where the Knowledge Space is not simply 'evidence -> knowledge' but can contain 'knowledge -> evidence -> inference -> knowledge', making knowledge a participating element in reasoning, not merely a final storage state.

rows.anchor: He explicitly shows that evidential probability 1 should not be treated as absolute certainty, and that treating evidence as permanently probability-1 creates an implausible monotonicity problem. New evidence can undermine something previously regarded as evidence.
rows.statement: Evidential probability 1 must not be treated as absolute certainty; treating evidence as permanently probability-1 creates an implausible monotonicity problem since new evidence can undermine something previously regarded as evidence. This validates Gärdenfors's distinction between historical evidence and permanently-unquestionable evidence: KnowledgeOS evidence history should be immutable, but epistemic status may be revised.

rows.anchor: Williamson's Chapter 11 argues for a **knowledge account of assertion**: the connection between knowing and asserting is not accidental.
rows.statement: Assertion is downstream from knowledge (knowledge account of assertion): the earlier model 'knowledge -> language' is refined to KNOWLEDGE -> warrant to assert -> ASSERTION -> language/communication. The sentence itself is not the knowledge; the assertion act is a consequence of an epistemic state and a communicative norm, close to Searle's distinction between descriptive and constitutive/performative language.

lineage_claims.quote: This changes our earlier model of language.

rows.anchor: ### K-INV-01 — Factivity cannot be silently violated
rows.statement: Seven proposed Kernel invariants: K-INV-01 Factivity cannot be silently violated (a record labelled 'knowledge' cannot silently mean merely belief/claim); K-INV-02 Representation is not knowledge (storage alone confers no epistemic status); K-INV-03 Knowledge attribution is contextual (must identify participant, scope/context, time); K-INV-04 Self-report is not self-proof ('I know P' is not sufficient proof P is known); K-INV-05 Evidence can be revisable (historical evidence records remain, interpretation can change); K-INV-06 Knowledge history is reconstructible (a current projection must be traceable to its inputs/transformations); K-INV-07 No assumption of epistemic transparency (the system must permit 'I don't know that I don't know P' and incomplete metaknowledge generally).

rows.anchor: ### Kernel should preserve
rows.statement: Proposed Kernel boundary (inside/outside/above): Inside Kernel — identity, participant, context, boundary, time, representation provenance, observation/source, proposition/content reference, knowledge attribution, epistemic transition, evidence/history, relationships, conflict, revision/supersession, question/inquiry, assessment history, regime reference. Outside Kernel — words, sentences, documents, embeddings, LLMs, vector databases, specific statistical models, possible-world machinery, Bayesian machinery, Pramāṇa implementation, Pāṇinian grammar, topic taxonomy, UI, search algorithm, explanation algorithm. Above the Kernel — knowledge projections, topics, answers, explanations, reports, architecture views, governance views, AI-agent views. Knowledge is present in the Kernel not as Truth+Belief+Evidence but as a KNOWLEDGE ATTRIBUTION (participant -> knows -> proposition -> context/time/boundary/regime), respecting primeness while remaining operational.

rows.anchor: The Kernel should not silently overwrite this into: P = KNOWLEDGE
rows.statement: The Kernel should NOT decide whether P is 'knowledge' universally. Example: for P='System X is secure', KnowledgeOS may preserve 'Alice claims to know P', 'Audit A provides evidence E', 'Regime R assesses P', 'Verification V says unresolved', 'Bob says not proven' as a KnowledgeAttribution(participant, proposition, context, time, regime, provenance) without collapsing to P=KNOWLEDGE, allowing different epistemologies/regimes to coexist and evaluate independently.

rows.anchor: Stop trying to construct "knowledge" bottom-up from representations.
rows.statement: The biggest insight: stop trying to construct knowledge bottom-up from representations (words->sentences->propositions->evidence->truth->knowledge is conceptually backwards). Instead: Infinite Knowledge Space -> Knowledge relation/state, which can be represented, asserted, justified, serve as evidence, influence action, or be revised/lost. Representation is a downstream expression of a knowledge-bearing state, not what creates knowledge. This also re-interprets the earlier S_t=P(Ω|A,B,L,U,R,t,H) formula: it is not 'the state of Knowledge itself' but 'a projected epistemic representation of knowledge at t', and K_t^A(P) becomes a knowledge attribution 'Agent A knows P at time t under the relevant context/regime.'

lineage_claims.quote: I would retain it, but change what it means.

rows.anchor: We should not seek: KnowledgeScore ∈ [0,1] as the first objective. Instead quantify **properties of knowledge**
rows.statement: Reject a universal KnowledgeScore ∈ [0,1]; instead quantify properties of knowledge Q(K,P,C,t) = (Evidence, Reliability, Margin, Coverage, Consistency, Relevance, Provenance, Stability). Candidate measurable properties: knowledge margin (how much nearby change before attribution fails), evidence contribution (removing evidence e, how much epistemic support changes — Williamson compares total-evidence hypothesis support against support after removing one item), explanatory value (how much knowing P improves prediction/explanation via probability/correlation), knowledge stability (how often an attribution is revised/lost under new evidence), projection coverage (how much declared scope has actually been represented).
missing: concrete formulas for each named property

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS must be able to represent uncertainty about its own epistemic boundary.
rows.statement: Do not try to make the Kernel completely transparent to itself (anti-luminosity applied to the system itself); a system claiming to know exactly what it knows and does not know makes an extremely strong assumption. KnowledgeOS must represent uncertainty about its own epistemic boundary via states: KNOWN, UNKNOWN, UNKNOWN WHETHER KNOWN, DISPUTED, OUTSIDE CURRENT MODEL, UNASSESSED — with 'unknown whether known' being particularly important.

lineage_claims.quote: This is a major correction to our previous model of `UNKNOWN`.

rows.anchor: The Knowledge Space is an unbounded space of reality, meaning, institutional structures, events, relations and propositions.
rows.statement: Final synthesis: 'The Knowledge Space is an unbounded space of reality, meaning, institutional structures, events, relations and propositions. Persons, machines and organizations have limited capacities and therefore form bounded, contextual, time-dependent projections of that space. Knowledge is a factive relation/state within such a projection—not merely information, representation, belief, evidence or truth alone. KnowledgeOS preserves the identities, contexts, provenance, temporal histories, epistemic transitions and knowledge attributions necessary for those projections to be reconstructed and evaluated under different regimes.' Capstone principle: KnowledgeOS must not confuse the projection with the space, the representation with the knowledge, or the epistemic assessment with reality — supported by McGinn, Floridi, Dretske, Fagin, Gärdenfors, Searle, and Williamson jointly.
invariants: never confuse projection with space, representation with knowledge, or assessment with reality

rows.anchor: I think we have now reached the point where the next step should be a formal KnowledgeOS meta-model and a brutal Zero-Lens falsification against real examples, rather than reading more philosophy.
rows.statement: Recommendation to move from reading more philosophy to producing a formal KnowledgeOS meta-model and a brutal Zero-Lens falsification against real examples, given the convergence reached across seven lenses/books.

rows.anchor: knowledge ≠ information... the transition requires a factive epistemic relation.
rows.statement: Combining Dretske's information flow (source->signal->information->representation) with Williamson (knowledge != information): information flow constitutes a possible epistemic input, but the transition to KNOWLEDGE additionally requires a factive epistemic relation — a more disciplined model than treating information flow as sufficient for knowledge.

rows.anchor: with **immutable historical transitions** but **mutable derived epistemic status**.
rows.statement: Combining Gärdenfors (expansion/revision/contraction/entrenchment) with Williamson (knowledge can be lost, isn't internally transparent, evidence can be undermined): a KNOWLEDGE HISTORY K1->K2(expansion)->K3(revision)->K4(contraction) has immutable historical transitions but mutable derived epistemic status — described as very close to the desired architecture.

rows.anchor: So Pramāṇa becomes a **knowledge-acquisition regime**, not Kernel ontology.
rows.statement: Different epistemic regimes may use different means of knowledge acquisition (perception, inference, analogy, testimony, etc. — Pramāṇa); Williamson's work tells us not to confuse 'how knowledge is acquired' with 'what knowledge fundamentally is', so Pramāṇa becomes a knowledge-acquisition regime, not Kernel ontology.

rows.anchor: Williamson: Do not reduce knowledge to simpler ingredients. Brandom: Model what knowledge-bearing discourse DOES: commit, justify, infer, challenge, revise, communicate.
rows.statement: Williamson's non-reduction result ('do not reduce knowledge to simpler ingredients') and Brandom's practice model ('model what knowledge-bearing discourse does: commit, justify, infer, challenge, revise, communicate') are explicitly declared complementary, not competing — together exactly what KnowledgeOS needs.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS may preserve computationally representable epistemic states without claiming that those states exhaust the philosophical nature of knowledge.
rows.statement: Gelfond & Kahl's computational model of an agent's represented beliefs does not contradict Williamson's non-reduction claim: it models computationally representable epistemic states, not a metaphysical analysis of knowledge itself. This distinction (computational representation vs philosophical exhaustiveness) should remain explicit in KnowledgeOS.

rows.anchor: Knows(a,p,t,c)
rows.statement: 'John knows that p' is a relation between a knower and an abstract proposition that can be true or false, surviving all lenses as Knows(a,p,t,c) (participant, proposition, time, context) — surprisingly close to the Williamson direction. But Brachman & Levesque add an operational separation Williamson did not give: KB(a) (operational representation) is not equivalent to Knows(a,p) (philosophical knowledge relation); the KB is a representation supporting reasoning about what the agent knows/believes — this is exactly where the KnowledgeOS Kernel should operate.
invariants: KB(a) is never equivalent to Knows(a,p)

rows.anchor: Williamson → what knowledge may fundamentally be. Brachman/Levesque → how knowledge can be operationally represented/reasoned about.
rows.statement: Explicit division of labor: Williamson tells us what knowledge may fundamentally be (factive relation); Brachman/Levesque tell us how knowledge can be operationally represented/reasoned about — the book does not itself establish the factive-relation claim. Final refined definitions: Knowledge is a factive epistemic relation between a participant and content about some domain, while a knowledge representation is a finite, context-dependent symbolic/structural projection of what the participant can make explicit and reason with, and may be incomplete relative to both the participant's broader knowledge and the unbounded Knowledge Space; Knowledge Space is the unbounded domain of possible facts/propositions/entities/relations/states/interpretations/institutional structures/inferential connections; KnowledgeOS preserves/manages finite time-dependent representations and epistemic histories while allowing multiple reasoning regimes to construct projections/derive implicit content/evaluate uncertainty/explain/compare views.

rows.anchor: ### T-3 · Is Knowledge the Kernel primitive? ... Position C is not a midpoint: it undercuts B's "must model the relationship" by denying that any analysis of knowing is available to model.
rows.statement: T-3 (is Knowledge the Kernel primitive) is now three-way, not two-way: Position A 'the Kernel is not knowledge' (120514) — Knowledge Space≠repository≠graph≠ontology; Position B 'Knowledge is not a possession — it is a relationship, a Kernel must model that relationship' (112051); Position C (new, Williamson via 162824) — knowing is primitive and unanalysable, stop reducing knowledge to information+truth+belief+evidence. Position C is not a midpoint between A and B: it undercuts B's 'must model the relationship' claim by denying any analysis of knowing is available to model at all. Neither side is K4; later research on both sides — no original-region document takes a position.

rows.anchor: Knowledge is a first-class architectural category, not merely a computed combination of lower-level metadata... it is a named external authority with an independent position... This is the only external, non-lineage evidence bearing on the corpus's most consequential internal disagreement (stored vs derived states)... Note law is on Williamson's side here: EpistemicState is a first-class Value object with seven enumerated states
rows.statement: Argues Williamson's position (knowledge as a first-class architectural category, not a computed combination of lower-level metadata) is the only external, non-lineage evidence bearing on the corpus's stored-vs-derived-states disagreement (opposing S1-F014's derived states and S1-F016's "identity is an administrative concern"), and is therefore under-weighted by being filed as ordinary RESEARCH ONLY alongside weaker material; notes law currently sides with Williamson, since EpistemicState is already a first-class Value object with seven enumerated states and no mechanism may ever produce certain of its members.

lexical.anchor: TRUE != BELIEVED != KNOWN / ASSERTED != ACCEPTED != TRUE / CONFIDENCE != TRUTH / UNKNOWN != FALSE ... Absence of knowledge must not be represented as falsehood.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The agent's **self-report of knowledge** is therefore an object of analysis, not a privileged oracle.
rationale_evidence.statement: For an AI agent claiming 'I know that the architecture decision is valid', KnowledgeOS should be able to represent P, the AI's claim knows(P), the supporting evidence, an external assessment (e.g. 'insufficient'), and the actual status ('unresolved') separately — the agent's self-report of knowledge is an object of analysis, not a privileged oracle.

sources.note: Step 225 (tail, phase_measure_theory): proposes the Step-182 Architecture Ledger -- a table (Element|Historical status|Evidence origin|Confidence|Reconstructed meaning|Future implication) as single source of truth for the transition from Steps 1-182 into the next architectural phase, framing the next open question as whether Semantic Integrity is truly the central invariant or a late compelling interpretation.

rows.anchor: Element | Historical status | Evidence origin | Confidence | Reconstructed meaning | Future implication
rows.statement: Step 225 (tail) proposes a formal Step-182 Architecture Ledger table (columns: Element, Historical status, Evidence origin, Confidence, Reconstructed meaning, Future implication) covering every major concept/component/principle/mathematical construct, to become the single source of truth for the transition from Steps 1-182 into the next architectural phase; only after this ledger exists should the numbered architectural sequence resume.

rows.anchor: Which principles survive the complete historical audit?
rows.statement: The next major open question posed at the close of Step 224/opening of Step 225: which principles survive the complete historical audit -- the point at which it can finally be decided whether Semantic Integrity is truly the architecture's central invariant, or merely a compelling interpretation that emerged late in the process.

rows.anchor: The strongest architecture that can be demonstrated to have existed or been explicitly established by the end of Step 182. ... A_H=EvidenceBound(Steps 1-182)
rows.statement: A_H (historical architecture) is defined precisely as the strongest architecture demonstrable to have existed or been explicitly established by the end of Step 182, formalized as A_H = EvidenceBound(Steps 1-182); the 'evidence-bound' qualifier means content appearing only in a later synthesis cannot automatically be inserted into A_H.

rows.anchor: H1 -- Explicitly established ... H2 -- Demonstrated ... H3 -- Strongly reconstructed ... H4 -- Candidate only ... Only H1-H3 belong in the historical baseline.
rows.statement: Four evidence classes for elements of A_H: H1 Explicitly established (E=Direct), H2 Demonstrated (via implementation/experiment/model/reproducible behavior, E=Demonstrated), H3 Strongly reconstructed (multiple independent historical observations converge, E=Convergent), H4 Candidate only (appears later as synthesis/analogy/interpretation, E=Candidate). Only H1-H3 belong in the historical baseline; H4 belongs in A_R or A_F.

rows.anchor: Status(A)=Supported with uncertainty.
rows.statement: The baseline must preserve uncertainty: evidence supporting a claim only probabilistically (e.g. conceptually P(A)=0.8) must not be converted into A=True, but recorded as Status(A)=Supported with uncertainty -- following directly from the epistemic architecture already developed.

rows.anchor: A_H(t) with A_1\rightarrow A_2\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow A_{182}. Step 182 is therefore a snapshot, not the whole history.
rows.statement: Historical architecture is temporal, not a single point A_182: it is better understood as A_H(t) evolving A_1->A_2->...->A_182, with Step 182 being a snapshot rather than the whole history -- the book's intellectual contribution may lie precisely in the transformation A_1->A_182.

rows.anchor: 1. When did it first appear? ... 7. What is its status at Step 182? This creates concept genealogy.
rows.statement: Architecture evolution should be represented explicitly per concept c(t_0)->c(t_1)->c(t_2) by answering seven questions (first appearance, producing problem, initial expression, whether/why modified, causal evidence for change, status at Step 182), creating a concept genealogy.

rows.anchor: Snapshot A_H^{182} ... Genealogy G_H ... A snapshot without genealogy produces the false impression that the architecture was designed top-down.
rows.statement: The baseline has two necessary structures: the Snapshot A_H^182 (what was established at the end) and the Genealogy G_H (how it developed); a snapshot alone falsely implies top-down design.

rows.anchor: X_{40}\rightarrow Y_{150}. The later interpretation remains visible. ... We must not rewrite Step 40 as if it had originally meant Y.
rows.statement: The historical baseline must contain no retrospective contamination: if Step 40 introduced X and Step 150's Y is later understood as a generalization of X, Step 40 must not be rewritten as if it originally meant Y -- instead record the visible chain X_40 -> Y_150.

rows.anchor: CurrentVocabulary\supset HistoricalVocabulary. ... SourceTerm\neq NormalizedTerm and NormalizedTerm\neq LaterTheory.
rows.statement: Because the current KnowledgeOS vocabulary is much richer than the historical vocabulary (CurrentVocabulary superset-of HistoricalVocabulary), terminology may be normalized for analysis but original terms must be preserved: SourceTerm != NormalizedTerm != LaterTheory. Formalized as a three-vocabulary model per concept: Historical term (what the work originally called it), Normalized term (common analytical vocabulary), Mature interpretation (what the later architecture understands it to mean) -- preventing semantic rewriting of history.

rows.anchor: A_H=(S,M,K,T,G,V,I)
rows.statement: The historical baseline is reconstructed along seven dimensions A_H=(S,M,K,T,G,V,I): S structural architecture, M semantic/domain architecture, K knowledge architecture, T temporal/version architecture, G governance architecture, V verification/assurance architecture, I implementation architecture.

rows.anchor: This is where DDD becomes central. We need to identify: bounded contexts; domain concepts; aggregates; invariants; translations; terminology; semantic boundaries.
rows.statement: Semantic architecture (M) asks what each important concept means and who owns that meaning -- the point where DDD becomes central, requiring identification of bounded contexts, domain concepts, aggregates, invariants, translations, terminology and semantic boundaries.

rows.anchor: Observation\rightarrow Evidence\rightarrow Interpretation\rightarrow Knowledge\rightarrow Decision. But this must only be included in A_H where Steps 1-182 support it.
rows.statement: Knowledge architecture (K) asks how the system knows something, with a potential lifecycle Observation->Evidence->Interpretation->Knowledge->Decision -- but this lifecycle may only enter A_H where Steps 1-182 actually support it, not by default.

rows.anchor: Dimension | Established by 182? | Evidence level | Main concepts | Open gaps
rows.statement: The final Step-182 baseline is proposed as a matrix over the seven dimensions (Structural, Semantic, Knowledge, Temporal, Governance, Assurance, Implementation) x (Established by 182?, Evidence level, Main concepts, Open gaps), deliberately left all-'?' until the historical audit is complete.

rows.anchor: AC_j=(Statement,Source,Evidence,Time,Status,Contradictions).
rows.statement: Every major architectural statement is to be recorded as an Architectural Claim AC_j = (Statement, Source, Evidence, Time, Status, Contradictions), e.g. AC_1: 'Every governed change requires evidence,' then classified as historically explicit, reconstructed, or future proposal.

rows.anchor: A0=Not established ... A1=Observed ... A2=Explicitly established ... A3=Demonstrated ... A4=Verified ... A5=Proposed extension.
rows.statement: Architecture claim status vocabulary: A0 Not established, A1 Observed, A2 Explicitly established, A3 Demonstrated, A4 Verified, A5 Proposed extension -- intended to give the book a rigorous epistemic structure.

rows.anchor: Established\neq Verified.
rows.statement: Established != Verified: an architectural rule (e.g. 'every artifact must have provenance') can be explicitly accepted (A2) while remaining unverified (A4=False) if no complete compliance mechanism exists.

rows.anchor: X\sim F_\theta might be A3 if it has been mathematically and experimentally demonstrated ... But it should not become: The architecture is fundamentally probabilistic.
rows.statement: Mathematical architecture receives the same A0-A5 status treatment: a construct like X~F_theta might earn A3 (Demonstrated) for a specific engineering problem without licensing the much stronger unqualified claim 'the architecture is fundamentally probabilistic' unless historical evidence actually supports it.

rows.anchor: InformationLoss\neq SemanticLoss automatically. Semantic loss requires domain relevance.
rows.statement: Information theory (H(X)=-sum p(x)log p(x), H(X)-H(Y), H(X|Y)) is a candidate formalization for information/semantic loss, but InformationLoss != SemanticLoss automatically -- semantic loss additionally requires domain relevance.

rows.anchor: R_C(K)\subseteq Recoverable(K') or explicitly declared loss. This is currently one of the strongest formal candidates for the KnowledgeOS architecture.
rows.statement: A stronger semantic-preservation formulation: for original knowledge K, transformed K'=T(K), and R_C(K) the distinctions relevant to context C, semantic preservation requires R_C(K) subseteq Recoverable(K') or explicitly declared loss -- rated currently one of the strongest formal candidates for the KnowledgeOS architecture.

rows.anchor: K_0\xrightarrow{T_1}K_1\xrightarrow{T_2}K_2\cdots\xrightarrow{T_n}K_n. T_i:(K_i,C_i,A_i,P_i)\rightarrow K_{i+1}.
rows.statement: The architecture-as-transformation-system model: K_0 -T1-> K_1 -T2-> K_2 -> ... -> K_n, with each transformation T_i:(K_i,C_i,A_i,P_i)->K_{i+1} parameterized by context C_i, authority A_i and provenance P_i -- beginning to unify the technical and mathematical architecture.

rows.anchor: Contract(T)=(Input,Preconditions,Transformation,Postconditions,PreservedSemantics,AllowedLoss,Evidence).
rows.statement: Each transformation is proposed to eventually carry a Contract(T) = (Input, Preconditions, Transformation, Postconditions, PreservedSemantics, AllowedLoss, Evidence) -- a potentially major architectural primitive applicable to AI generation, document conversion, API translation, code generation, architecture transformation, and governance workflows.

rows.anchor: Transformation+Contract+Evidence becomes a reusable assurance mechanism.
rows.statement: Deterministic assurance: a transformation verified against Precondition, Postcondition and PreservationInvariant makes Transformation+Contract+Evidence a reusable assurance mechanism.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS governs transformations of engineering knowledge while preserving the semantic, epistemic, temporal and governance properties required by their receiving contexts. ... it remains A_R until the historical audit establishes that this interpretation genuinely emerges from Steps 1-182.
rows.statement: Candidate deeper reframing of KnowledgeOS: rather than 'KnowledgeOS stores engineering knowledge', it may be 'KnowledgeOS governs transformations of engineering knowledge while preserving the semantic, epistemic, temporal and governance properties required by their receiving contexts' -- a stronger architectural statement explicitly classified as A_R (reconstructed, not yet historically established) pending audit.

rows.anchor: Chapter 1\rightarrow Conflict/Uncertainty ... Chapter 4\rightarrow Knowledge/Continuity. But each mapping must be marked P1, P2, or P3.
rows.statement: Candidate Gita chapter mapping (interpretive lens, not architectural dependency, reconstructed independently as A_H first): Chapter 1 -> Conflict/Uncertainty, Chapter 2 -> Identity/Change, Chapter 3 -> Action/Responsibility, Chapter 4 -> Knowledge/Continuity, each mapping required to carry a P1/P2/P3 classification.

rows.anchor: The engineering investigation developed its concepts through practical, mathematical and architectural work. Chapters 1-4 of the Gita later provide a philosophical lens through which certain structural similarities can be examined.
rows.statement: The crucial literary rule: the book must never imply 'the KnowledgeOS architecture was derived from the Gita' unless the historical record proves it; the safe framing is that the engineering investigation developed its concepts independently and the Gita chapters later provide a philosophical lens for examining structural similarities.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS=Knowledge Transformation Governance operating across Semantic+Epistemic+Temporal+Governance with Transformation\rightarrow Contract\rightarrow Verification\rightarrow Evidence. ... Observe\rightarrow Interpret\rightarrow Decide\rightarrow Act\rightarrow Verify\rightarrow Learn.
rows.statement: Step 225's provisional candidate reconstructed model: KnowledgeOS = Knowledge Transformation Governance, operating across Semantic+Epistemic+Temporal+Governance dimensions via Transformation->Contract->Verification->Evidence, embedded in a system feedback loop Observe->Interpret->Decide->Act->Verify->Learn -- explicitly not yet declared the final architecture.

rows.anchor: Every architectural claim must carry its provenance and epistemic status. ... Claim\rightarrow Source\rightarrow Evidence\rightarrow Interpretation\rightarrow Status. And ultimately: Architecture\rightarrow Evidence\rightarrow Verification.
rows.statement: Step 225 verdict: the most important result is not another formula but an architectural epistemology -- every architectural claim must carry its provenance and epistemic status, giving Claim->Source->Evidence->Interpretation->Status and ultimately Architecture->Evidence->Verification -- the discipline required before accepting the emerging Semantic Integrity/Knowledge Transformation architecture as final theory.

sources.note: Step 122: an agent-executable eight-stage evidence protocol (Claim->Locate->Inspect->Trace->Test->Observe->Classify->Report) turning the prior architecture-conformance method into an operational Claude/Codex-shared discipline, with traceability-strength scale T0-T4, epistemic classification FACT/INFERENCE/TARGET/GAP, confidence scale C0-C4, negative-evidence rule, anti-hallucination stopping rule, bypass-test matrix against the C1-C7 constitution, a ten-item agent execution contract, an Evidence Execution Report template, an AgentAssuranceScore metric, and a closing self-governance loop (ConstitutionalHealthCheck, ConstitutionalDrift).

rows.anchor: Claim → Locate → Inspect → Trace → Test → Observe → Classify → Report
rows.statement: Defines EEP = {E1..E8}: an eight-stage mandatory pipeline (Claim, Locate, Inspect, Trace, Test, Observe, Classify, Report) that an agent must explicitly state it performed (not necessarily at equal depth) before making an architectural claim; the governing principle is 'an agent must prove an architectural claim from evidence; it must not prove it from plausibility.'

rows.anchor: Structural / Behavioral / Governance / Temporal / Assurance / Operational
rows.statement: E1 Claim requires a precise, falsifiable proposition (contrasts 'Understand KnowledgeOS' [bad] with a typed claim like 'AuthoritativeDecision -> Provenance' [good]) and distinguishes six claim types: Structural (component depends on component), Behavioral (creating an authoritative object requires provenance), Governance (only an authorized actor can approve), Temporal (superseded decisions excluded from current knowledge), Assurance (rule X deterministically verified), Operational (runtime state fed back into KnowledgeOS).

rows.anchor: NotFound(Location) ≠ Absent(System)
rows.statement: E2 Locate names search targets (README, docs/, ADR/, architecture/, src/, tests/, schemas/, migrations/, config/, CI/CD, hooks/, agents/, runtime configuration) and states the negative-evidence rule: finding nothing in one location does not prove system-wide absence; the agent must report 'no evidence found in the inspected locations' rather than 'the capability does not exist.'

rows.anchor: DeclaredArchitecture ... ImplementedArchitecture ... VerifiedBehavior
rows.statement: E3 Inspect distinguishes evidence types by artifact kind: documentation establishes DeclaredArchitecture, source code establishes ImplementedArchitecture, tests establish VerifiedBehavior — these are different evidence types and must not be conflated.

rows.anchor: The objective is not simply finding matching names. It is establishing semantic linkage.
rows.statement: E4 Trace: given a claim Decision -> Implementation, the agent follows the chain Decision -> ADR/record -> change request -> PR -> commit -> artifact -> deployment, aiming at semantic linkage rather than textual name-matching; defines traceability-strength scale T0 (no link) < T1 (textual similarity) < T2 (explicit reference) < T3 (machine-readable identifier) < T4 (verified causal/implementation relationship), e.g. an ADR-042 identifier appearing in a commit is stronger evidence than shared wording.

rows.anchor: Static / Unit / Integration / Architecture / Deployment / Runtime
rows.statement: E5 Test: for a behavioral claim (e.g. 'authoritative knowledge cannot be created without provenance'), execute a concrete test (create(authoritative=true, provenance=null) expecting Reject) and classify it on a six-level test hierarchy (Static, Unit, Integration, Architecture, Deployment, Runtime) since the test type affects what the result actually proves.

rows.anchor: Static code is not enough for operational claims.
rows.statement: E6 Observe: operational claims (e.g. 'Nexus runs rootless') require inspecting actual runtime/deployment/logs/metrics/events, not merely a static configuration file such as a Podman config.

rows.anchor: FACT | INFERENCE | TARGET | GAP
rows.statement: E7 Classify: every finding receives one of four epistemic classifications — FACT (directly evidenced, e.g. a Containerfile using a specified base image, via E2/E3), INFERENCE (a reasoned interpretation that must not be presented as established fact without stronger evidence, e.g. 'this repo appears to implement the Evidence bounded context'), TARGET (intended future architecture unless implementation proves otherwise, e.g. 'KnowledgeOS should provide closed-loop governance'), GAP (Expected ≠ Observed, e.g. architecture requires provenance but authoritative records can currently be created without it).

rows.anchor: CLAIM / FACTS / EVIDENCE / INFERENCE / VERIFICATION / GAP / TARGET / CONFIDENCE
rows.statement: E8 Report: the final report must never collapse evidence into one narrative; it uses a fixed section format (Claim, Facts, Evidence, Inference, Verification, Gap, Target, Confidence) 'to prevent architectural contamination,' illustrated with a worked standard-agent-output example ending in STATUS: CONFORMANT / CONFIDENCE: HIGH.

rows.anchor: C0=Unknown, C1=Weak, C2=Moderate, C3=Strong, C4=Verified
rows.statement: Proposes a five-level ordinal confidence scale (C0 Unknown .. C4 Verified) as superior to arbitrary percentages; argues LLMConfidence ≠ EvidenceConfidence because an LLM stating '95% confident' does not establish a quantitative probability, whereas evidence-derived confidence must derive from evidence quality; also distinguishes EvidenceStrength from Confidence (strong evidence can still leave interpretive ambiguity).

rows.anchor: If evidence is insufficient, the agent MUST preserve UNKNOWN.
rows.statement: States an agent stopping rule / anti-hallucination rule: when evidence is insufficient the agent must preserve UNKNOWN rather than fill the gap from general knowledge; explicitly frames stopping with disclosed uncertainty (e.g. 'implementation is supported, enforcement is unverified') as a successful investigation, not a failure.

rows.anchor: Mode A — Architecture reconstruction ... Mode E — Knowledge reconstruction
rows.statement: Defines five repository investigation modes with distinct evidence focus — A Architecture reconstruction (Structure+Dependencies), B Governance verification (Authority+Decision+Process), C Assurance verification (Rule+Test+Evidence), D Runtime verification (Deployment+Observation), E Knowledge reconstruction (Meaning+Provenance+Validity) — and requires the agent to select the mode before searching, and to follow a Broad->Narrow->Exact->Trace search strategy (e.g. 'provenance' -> 'source_id' -> 'createKnowledge' -> tests -> runtime).

rows.anchor: Can the invariant be bypassed?
rows.statement: Warns against name-based conclusions (e.g. a class named ProvenanceService does not itself prove provenance is enforced — the agent must ask who calls it, when, what happens on failure, whether the result is persisted, and whether it can be bypassed); defines the enforcement test 'can the invariant be bypassed? If yes, Enforcement<Strong,' illustrated by Experiment 2 where a ProvenanceService exists but developers can insert DB records without provenance, yielding Declared=Yes, Enforced=No, verdict PARTIAL.

rows.anchor: C1 ... provenance required ... direct persistence | C7 ... feedback path exists ... finding dead-end
rows.statement: Extends the Step 120 C1-C7 constitution with a bypass-question and bypass-test matrix per invariant: C1 can authoritative knowledge bypass provenance via direct persistence; C2 can approval bypass authority via unauthorized promotion; C3 can inference be promoted to authority without validation; C4 can stale knowledge appear current via stale retrieval; C5 can verification results be fabricated/irreproducible via inconsistent rerun; C6 can governed actions occur without traceability via untracked action; C7 can findings disappear without governance closure via finding dead-end — presented as a practical assurance test suite.

rows.anchor: 1. State the claim. ... 10. Never promote inference to authority.
rows.statement: Defines a ten-item 'agent execution contract' every KnowledgeOS-aware engineering agent must follow: state the claim; identify evidence sources; inspect implementation; trace relationships; execute relevant tests where possible; inspect runtime where required; separate fact from inference; report uncertainty; identify gaps; never promote inference to authority.

rows.anchor: SameAuthority / SameEvidenceRules / SameConstitution / SameEpistemicDiscipline
rows.statement: Proposes that Claude and Codex should share the Evidence Execution Protocol as a common agent-instruction layer: the important symmetry is not identical configuration but SameAuthority, SameEvidenceRules, SameConstitution, SameEpistemicDiscipline, while Claude and Codex harnesses remain operationally different — diagrammed as KnowledgeOS -> Evidence Protocol -> {Claude Harness, Codex Harness} -> Same Truth.

rows.anchor: This is a pointer/behavior contract, not a duplicate knowledge repository.
rows.statement: Sketches a minimal KnowledgeOS-aware AGENTS.md operating contract (consult authoritative sources, verify current validity, preserve provenance, distinguish fact from inference, use deterministic checks where available, record material engineering actions against authorization, never treat local agent memory as authoritative) and states that .claude/ and .codex/ should likewise hold tools/hooks/workflow/session-behavior/verification-procedures/pointers-to-KnowledgeOS but must not become the enterprise architecture authority themselves — the goal is OperationalSymmetry without KnowledgeDuplication.

rows.anchor: # Evidence Execution Report ... Open questions: ...
rows.statement: Specifies a standard 'Evidence Execution Report' template with fields Claim, Scope, Evidence inspected, Implementation, Tests executed, Runtime observations, FACT, INFERENCE, TARGET, GAP, Conformance, Confidence, Open questions, as the mandatory end-of-investigation deliverable.

rows.anchor: AgentAssuranceScore = f(EvidenceCompleteness, Traceability, Verification, EpistemicDiscipline)
rows.statement: Proposes judging an agent by EvidenceQuality rather than AnswerQuality: an articulate but unsupported answer should score poorly, a cautious evidence-backed answer highly; defines AgentAssuranceScore = f(EvidenceCompleteness, Traceability, Verification, EpistemicDiscipline), explicitly preferable to measuring only LLMAnswerSimilarity; further defines Completeness = VerifiedLinks/RequiredLinks for a claim needing n evidence links, notes critical missing links should carry higher weight (WeightedCompleteness preferable to plain Completeness), and gives Authority as an example of a critical link whose absence should not be masked by ten present technical links.

rows.anchor: Claim ├── supportedBy → Evidence ... └── classifiedAs → Status
rows.statement: Observes that an agent's own investigation becomes graph data (Claim -supportedBy-> Evidence, -verifiedBy-> Test, -observedAt-> Runtime, -interpretedAs-> Finding, -classifiedAs-> Status), so the process of understanding the architecture itself becomes part of KnowledgeOS knowledge.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS can use its own evidence protocol to verify KnowledgeOS.
rows.statement: States the recursive property KnowledgeOS -> SelfObservation -> SelfVerification ('the beginning of self-assuring architecture'), with a worked self-verification example: for the claim 'every authoritative decision has provenance,' KnowledgeOS runs Query: AuthoritativeDecision WHERE Provenance=NULL, gets result 0, and concludes C1=PASS — argued to be far stronger than documentation merely asserting the property.

rows.anchor: C1 Provenance PASS ... C7 Feedback FAIL
rows.statement: Proposes a periodic ConstitutionalHealthCheck evaluating C1..C7 with a PASS/WARN/FAIL dashboard per invariant, framed as ArchitectureHealth = f(C1..C7); explicitly warns against reducing the constitution to a single aggregate score (e.g. 87%) since that can conceal a catastrophic failure in one invariant such as authority — the individual invariants must remain primary.

rows.anchor: C1: PASS → FAIL ... This is ConstitutionalDrift.
rows.statement: Defines ConstitutionalDrift: if an implementation previously satisfied an invariant (e.g. C1) and a later release regresses it (e.g. allows provenance-free records), the transition PASS->FAIL is itself something that should become an observable event, not merely a silent state change.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS → ConstitutionalCheck → Finding → Governance → Remediation → Verification → KnowledgeOS
rows.statement: Closes Step 122 with a self-governance loop diagram: KnowledgeOS -> ConstitutionalCheck -> Finding -> Governance -> Remediation -> Verification -> back to KnowledgeOS, described as 'the system applying its own operating principles to itself' / 'a self-observing system,' and boxes the final verdict that the EEP (Claim..Report pipeline plus FACT/INFERENCE/TARGET/GAP classification plus constitutional bypass testing) gives Claude and Codex a common engineering-evidence discipline without duplicating KnowledgeOS knowledge into local harnesses.

rows.anchor: ArchitectureRule → ExecutableCheck.
rows.statement: States 'constitution as executable architecture': architecture ceases to be merely descriptive and becomes partially executable (ArchitectureRule -> ExecutableCheck), the same principle underlying the deterministic assurance model, diagrammed as KnowledgeOS Constitution -> Machine Rules -> Test Suite -> Evidence -> Constitutional State; a 'self-verifying agent harness' lets Claude/Codex run 'Verify KnowledgeOS constitution' and receive a per-invariant PASS/WARN/PARTIAL state to use as operating context — but the agent must not itself decide an invariant is unimportant and ignore it; severity/exception rules must themselves be governed.

rows.anchor: What are your governing principles? ... What is currently failing?
rows.statement: Concludes the architecture is 'becoming self-describing' — able to potentially answer 'what are your governing principles,' 'are you currently conformant,' 'which evidence proves that,' and 'what is currently failing' — a substantially different capability from a documentation platform; boxes the Step 123 verdict: KnowledgeOS can become a subject of its own assurance model (KOS-SV-01..SV-07 covering Provenance/Authority/EpistemicStatus/TemporalValidity/DeterministicAssurance/Traceability/Feedback).

sources.note: Live, progressively-populated verifier matrix (skeleton 2026-08-29, updated 2026-08-30) mapping every corpus step (001-222+) to its source file(s), original title, verification batch, verification status, and gap/anomaly notes. Records corpus growth as a first-class fact (chronology is evidence; earlier findings retained as time-indexed even when later superseded), and aggregates the corpus's recurring defect patterns: fabricated tool-transcript results, colliding invariant/evidence-scale namespaces, byte-identical duplicate files, an all-'?' unfilled-matrix pattern, and a handful of 'supervisory correction' interventions.

rows.statement: Row lifecycle vocabulary for the traceability matrix: each step row moves TRACED (batch record exists) -> VERIFIED (independent reconstruction done, recorded in a STEP-VERIFY-* file) with a final per-concept category: RETAINED / REFINED / REPLACED / REJECTED / SUPERSEDED / INCORPORATED / STILL OPEN / LOST-UNACCOUNTED.

rows.anchor: This supersedes the earlier finding TV-F-041 that Step 208 was NON-EXISTENT ... The earlier record was correct at its timestamp and is retained as a time-indexed observation, not deleted -- chronology is evidence.
rows.statement: Corpus-growth handling principle: because the corpus is live and grows during verification (Steps 206-215 were written during this very verification session), a finding correct at its recorded timestamp (e.g. 'Step 208 NON-EXISTENT' at 01:12) is retained rather than deleted when later falsified by growth (Step 208 written at 01:18) -- chronology itself is evidence.
